title: "Whom Shall I Send?"
paragraphs:
"Whom Shall I Send?"
The Divine Question That Still Echoes Through Heaven—and Into Your Heart
There are moments when heaven becomes so real that every excuse we have spent a lifetime building suddenly collapses into silence.
Not because God raises His voice.
But because His holiness reveals who we truly are.
Isaiah experienced one of those moments.
It was not merely a vision.
It was an encounter that shattered a man before it transformed him.
"In the year that King Uzziah died..." (Isaiah 6:1)
The nation was grieving. Stability had vanished. A powerful king was gone. Fear filled the future.
Yet while everyone else was staring at an empty throne on earth, Isaiah looked up—and saw a throne that had never been vacant.
"I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up..." (Isaiah 6:1)
Human kingdoms rise.
Human leaders fall.
But the King of Heaven has never once stood up from His throne because He has never lost control.
Then Isaiah saw what words can barely contain.
The seraphim surrounded the throne crying,

קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ
(Qādôsh, qādôsh, qādôsh.)
"Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory." (Isaiah 6:3)
The Hebrew word קָדוֹשׁ (qādôsh) means far more than morally pure.
It means completely set apart.
Utterly incomparable.
Perfect beyond imagination.
The repetition three times is not poetic exaggeration.
In Hebrew, repetition expresses emphasis.
To say "holy" three times is Scripture's way of declaring that no language is sufficient to describe God's absolute perfection.
The foundations shook.
Smoke filled the temple.
Creation itself trembled before its Creator.
Yet Isaiah's first reaction was not excitement.
It was terror.
"Woe is me! For I am undone..." (Isaiah 6:5)
The Hebrew word translated "undone" is נִדְמֵיתִי (nidmêṯî).
It carries the sense of being ruined, destroyed, completely exposed.
Isaiah did not compare himself with other people.
He compared himself with God.
That changes everything.
The closer we come to God's holiness, the less impressive our own goodness appears.
Many people today ask why they do not hear God's voice.
Perhaps the deeper question is whether we have first allowed His holiness to reveal our need.
Because before God sends anyone, He first transforms them.
Then something astonishing happened.
A seraph flew with a live coal taken from the altar.
It touched Isaiah's lips.
"Your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for." (Isaiah 6:7)
Notice carefully.
Isaiah never asked for forgiveness.
He confessed his condition.
God Himself provided the cleansing.
Grace always begins with God.
This scene points beyond itself.
The burning coal from the altar foreshadows the ultimate sacrifice that would come centuries later in Jesus Christ.
The altar temporarily covered sin.
The cross removed it.
The Hebrew verb translated "atoned for" is כָּפַר (kāpar).
In the Old Testament it carries the idea of covering or making reconciliation.
But the New Testament reveals its complete fulfillment through Christ.
When Jesus declared,
Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai)
"It is finished." (John 19:30)
He announced that the work of redemption had been completed in full.
Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai) was a commercial term meaning a debt had been paid completely.
Nothing remained unpaid.
No additional sacrifice would ever be necessary.
This is why the Gospel is not about people trying harder.
It is about trusting the One who finished what we never could.
Only after Isaiah experienced cleansing did heaven speak.
Then came one of the most famous questions in all of Scripture.
"Whom shall I send, and who will go for Us?" (Isaiah 6:8)
Notice something remarkable.
God already knew the answer.
The question was never asked because heaven lacked information.
It was asked because God invites willing hearts into His mission.
The Hebrew reads,

אֶת־מִי אֶשְׁלַח וּמִי יֵלֶךְ־לָנוּ
('Et-mi eshlaḥ umi yēlekh-lānû?)
Literally,
"Whom shall I send? And who will go for Us?"
The emphasis is not simply on movement.
It is on representation.
The one who goes carries the message and authority of the One who sends.
Isaiah answered,

הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
(Hinneni, shelacheni.)
"Here am I; send me."
The word הִנְנִי (hinneni) means much more than "I'm here."
It means,
"I am completely available."
"My life belongs to You."
"Whatever You ask, my answer is already yes."
This is one of the most beautiful words in the Hebrew Scriptures.
Abraham said hinneni.
Jacob said hinneni.
Moses said hinneni.
Samuel said hinneni.
Isaiah said hinneni.
It is the language of surrendered hearts.
The New Testament echoes this same truth.
Jesus told His disciples,
"The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few." (Matthew 9:37)
God's greatest shortage has never been power.
It has always been willing people.
The astonishing reality is that God does not primarily call the most talented.
He calls the surrendered.
Grace does not merely rescue us from sin.
Grace recruits us into God's redemptive work.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus did not simply save us from something.
He saved us for Someone.
The Apostle Paul writes,
"We are therefore Christ's ambassadors..." (2 Corinthians 5:20)
The Greek word is πρεσβεύομεν (presbeuomen)—we serve as official representatives of the King.
Every believer is sent.
Some across oceans.
Some across neighborhoods.
Some across dinner tables.
Some across office desks.
Some into hospitals.
Some into classrooms.
Some into broken families.
Some into lonely friendships.
Every disciple is a messenger.
Perhaps today heaven's ancient question still echoes across eternity.
Not because God is searching for workers.
But because He is searching for surrendered hearts.
Perhaps you have believed your failures disqualified you.
So did Isaiah.
Perhaps your past feels too shameful.
The cross says otherwise.
Perhaps you think God only uses extraordinary people.
Scripture consistently tells another story.
God delights in transforming ordinary people into extraordinary testimonies of His grace.
The Bible is filled with scandal rewritten by grace.
Moses the murderer became God's deliverer.
Rahab the prostitute became part of the Messiah's family line.
Peter the denier became a fearless preacher.
Paul the persecutor became an apostle.
And above all, sinners become children of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
The greatest miracle is not that God finds perfect people.
It is that He perfects His work through forgiven people.
Maybe the question is no longer whether God is calling.
Maybe the question is whether we are still listening.
Comment, "Here am I, Lord." If you are still struggling, comment, "Pray for me." Your words may become the encouragement another believer desperately needed today.
One surrendered heart can become the answer to a prayer someone else has been waiting for.
